There are numerous occasions when the first step of proving some result is a verification for relatively simple case, this strategy can be justified if one is able to control of "maximal error" from the simple case to the general case, known as "density argument". We will follow this approach to develop Lebesgue differentiation theorem. Finally we explore the relationship between measures and classical derivatives, via the important Lebesgue-Radon-Nikodym theorem.
The major reference for this note is Terry's notes for both 254A and 254B.

1.1. Littlewood's three principles

In analysis, one often considers a class of objects that can be, under some criterion, approximated by objects in a more restrictive but simpler subclass. For instances,

  • Any real number can be approximated by a sequence of rational numbers, in the sense that the absolute value of the difference coverges to zero, namely convergence in the Euclidean norm.
  • The class L1(Rn) {L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}L1(Rn) of extended real-valued Lebesgue integrable functions (more correctly, their equivalent classes) on Rn {\mathbb{R}^{n}}Rn is defined to be the measurable funcitons can be approximated by the subclass of simple functions on Rn {\mathbb{R}^{n}}Rn, where one asks for the convergence of the integral of simple functions to converge to a real number, namely the convergence in L1 {L^{1}}L1-norm ∥⋅∥1 {\|\cdot\|_{1}}∥⋅∥1​.

It is evident that

{step functions}⊂{simple functions}⊂L1(Rn).\displaystyle \text{\{step functions}\}\subset\text{\{simple functions}\}\subset L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{n}).{step functions}⊂{simple functions}⊂L1(Rn).

By construction, the family of simple functions is in dense in L1(Rn) {L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}L1(Rn). The family of step functions is also dense in the family of simple functions, which follows from the regulariy of Lebesgue measurable sets:

Lemma 1 (Littlewood's First principle) Let M {\mathfrak{M}}M be the σ {\sigma}σ-algebra of Lebesgue measurable sets in Rn {\mathbb{R}^{n}}Rn. Then for any E∈M {E\in\mathfrak{M}}E∈M, there exist an open set G {G}G and closed set F {F}F with F⊂E⊂G {F\subset E\subset G}F⊂E⊂G and μ(G−F)<ϵ {\mu(G-F)<\epsilon}μ(G−F)<ϵ.
Since closed sets in Rn {\mathbb{R}^{n}}Rn are σ {\sigma}σ-compact, so in particular if μ(E)<∞ {\mu(E)<\infty}μ(E)<∞ we can choose F {F}F to be compact (this is the inner regularity of Lebesgue measurable sets). Consequently, there exist an Fσ {F_{\sigma}}Fσ​ set A {A}A and a Gδ {G_{\delta}}Gδ​ set B {B}B such that A⊂F⊂B {A\subset F\subset B}A⊂F⊂B and μ(B−A)=0 {\mu(B-A)=0}μ(B−A)=0.

In fact, the Lebesgue outer measure μ∗ {\mu_{*}}μ∗​ defines a pesudometric on the set of subsets of Rn {\mathbb{R}^{n}}Rn, namely, by defining

d(A,B)=μ∗(AΔB)\displaystyle d(A,B)=\mu_{*}(A\Delta B)d(A,B)=μ∗​(AΔB)

where Δ {\Delta}Δ refers to symmetric difference of the two sets. The pseudometic thus defines a topology on P(Rn) {\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}P(Rn). Here one also sees the role played by the measure zero sets. The Lebesgue σ {\sigma}σ-algebra M {\mathfrak{M}}M is the completion of Borel σ {\sigma}σ-algebra B {\mathcal{B}}B on Rn {\mathbb{R}^{n}}Rn with respect to the pseudometric. In particular M {\mathfrak{M}}M is complete, and is in fact unique in the sense of extension, thanks to Hahn-Kolmogorov extension theorem. In this spirit, we also have:

Theorem 2 (Riesz-Fischer) L1(Rn) {L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}L1(Rn) is a Banach space with respect to ∥⋅∥1 {\|\cdot\|_{1}}∥⋅∥1​. More generally, Lp(Rn) {L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}Lp(Rn) is complete with respect to ∥⋅∥p {\|\cdot\|_{p}}∥⋅∥p​ for 1≤p≤∞ {1\leq p\leq\infty}1≤p≤∞.

Combined with the Lemma 1, we have the following compeletion with respect to ∥⋅∥1 {\|\cdot\|_{1}}∥⋅∥1​-norm

{step functions}‾={simple functions}‾=L1(Rn).(1) \displaystyle \overline{\text{\{step functions}\}}=\overline{\text{\{simple functions}\}}=L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{n}). (1){step functions}​={simple functions}​=L1(Rn).(1)

On the other hand, in light of Riesz representation theorem, one can also approximate measurable functions with continuous functions of compact support. Thus we also have another completion with respect to ∥⋅∥1 {\|\cdot\|_{1}}∥⋅∥1​-norm

{Cc(Rn)}‾=L1(Rn).\displaystyle \overline{\{C_{c}(\mathbb{R}^{n})\}}=L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{n}).{Cc​(Rn)}​=L1(Rn).

This fact is illustrated in

Theorem 3 (Littlewood's second principle) Let f∈L1(Rn) {f\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}f∈L1(Rn). Then for any ϵ>0 {\epsilon>0}ϵ>0, there exists a compactly supported continuous function g∈Cc(Rn) {g\in C_{c}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}g∈Cc​(Rn) such that

∥f−g∥1<ϵ.\displaystyle \|f-g\|_{1}<\epsilon.∥f−g∥1​<ϵ.

Proof: In view of (1), we only need to do it for the indicator function χE {\chi_{E}}χE​ for some measurable E {E}E with μ(E)<∞ {\mu(E)<\infty}μ(E)<∞. Apply Lemma 1, we have an open set G {G}G and a compact set K {K}K such that K⊂E⊂G {K\subset E\subset G}K⊂E⊂G and μ(G−K)<ϵ {\mu(G-K)<\epsilon}μ(G−K)<ϵ. Now use Urysohn's lemma. □ \Box□

The above can be roughly summerised as "measurable sets are not so different from open and closed sets in terms of taking their measures; integrable functions are not so different from simple functions in terms of taking their integrals''. This can be also applied to "mode of convergence'': Given a pointwise almost everywhere converging sequence of measurable functions, away from an exceptional set that is small, one can control at least locally its mode of convergence.
We say that fn:Rn→R {f_{n}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}}fn​:Rn→R converges locally uniformly to f:Rn→R {f:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}}f:Rn→R if for every compact set K⊂Rn {K\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}}K⊂Rn, fn {f_{n}}fn​ converges uniformly to f {f}f.

Theorem 5 (Lusin's theorem) Let f {f}f be a measurable function on Rn {\mathbb{R}^{n}}Rn. Then for any ϵ>0 {\epsilon>0}ϵ>0, there exists a measurable set Aϵ⊂Rn {A_{\epsilon}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}}Aϵ​⊂Rn such that μ(Aϵ)<ϵ {\mu(A_{\epsilon})<\epsilon}μ(Aϵ​)<ϵ and f⇂Rn−Aϵ {f\downharpoonright_{\mathbb{R}^{n}-A_{\epsilon}}}f⇂Rn−Aϵ​​ is continuous.

Of course, all our discussion above can be applied to the situation where Rn {\mathbb{R}^{n}}Rn is replaced by a σ {\sigma}σ-compact LCH space, where all measurable sets are inner regular.

It is sometimes useful to use semi-continuous functions due to their generality.

1.2. Density argument: Lebesgue differentiation theorem

The power of Littlewood's principles not only lies in helping one to understand the behavior of various "Lebesgue'' type of contructions, e.g. measurable sets, functions only defined almost everywhere etc., but also allow one to attack a problem first by looking at a "simpler version'', namely the subject class being replaced by one of its dense subclasses. Consider the following statement concerning the translation invariance of Lebesgue measure: If m {m}m is a Borel measure defined on (Rn,B) {(\mathbb{R}^{n},\mathcal{B})}(Rn,B) and is translational invariant, then there is a positive constant λ>0 {\lambda>0}λ>0 such that

m(E)=λLn(E)\displaystyle m(E)=\lambda\mathcal{L}^{n}(E)m(E)=λLn(E)

for all E∈B {E\in\mathcal{B}}E∈B. By finite additivity and translation invariance, we see that the conclusion obviously hold for dyadic meshes, i.e. the cubes with sides of length 2n {2^{n}}2n, n∈Z {n\in\mathbb{Z}}n∈Z. Since dyadic meshes are dense in the space of measurable sets, using Fatou's lemma, we see that the result holds by taking limit. In this subsection we are interested in the following convergence theorem, a generalization of the first fundamental theorem of calculus:

Theorem 11 (Lebesgue differentiation theorem) Let f:Rn→R {f:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}}f:Rn→R be absolutely integrable. Then for almost every x∈Rn {x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}x∈Rn,

lim⁡r→0+1Ln(B(x,r))∫B(x,r)∣f(y)−f(x)∣dy=0(2) \displaystyle \lim_{r\rightarrow0^{+}}\frac{1}{\mathcal{L}^{n}(B(x,r))}\int_{B(x,r)}\left|f(y)-f(x)\right|dy=0 (2)r→0+lim​Ln(B(x,r))1​∫B(x,r)​∣f(y)−f(x)∣dy=0(2)

The point x∈Rn {x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}x∈Rn such that (2) holds is called a Lebesgue point of f {f}f. Thus, for f∈L1(Rn) {f\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}f∈L1(Rn), almost every point is a Lebesgue point of f {f}f.

There are in general two ingredients to prove such converging result, known as density argument:

  1. Verification of the statement for objects in the dense subclass;
  2. A quantitative estimate that bounds the "maximal error''.

It is easy to verify Theorem 11 for continuous compactly supported functions on Rn {\mathbb{R}^{n}}Rn, which form a dense subclass of L1(Rn) {L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}L1(Rn). In the following we will develop the corresponding quantitative estimates. The first one is Markov inequality.

We can in fact get a slightly more precise Lebesgue decomposition than the one above. Let X {X}X be such that every point is measurable. We say a measure μ {\mu}μ is continuous if μ({x})=0 {\mu(\{x\})=0}μ({x})=0 for all x∈X {x\in X}x∈X. Let μ,λ {\mu,\lambda}μ,λ be as above, and furthermore μ {\mu}μ is continuous, then there is a unique decompostion

where λac≪μ {\lambda_{ac}\ll\mu}λac​≪μ, λsc {\lambda_{sc}}λsc​ is singular to μ {\mu}μ and continuous, and λpp {\lambda_{pp}}λpp​ suppoted on an at most countable set. Here, λsc {\lambda_{sc}}λsc​, λpp {\lambda_{pp}}λpp​ are called singular continuous and pure point components of λ {\lambda}λ respectively. The decomposition for the case of unsigned measures above (later it extends to the signed case as well) is analogous to the decomposition of monotone function in the 1-dimensional case. Recall that if F:R→R {F:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}}F:R→R is non-decreasing, then the only discontinuities of F {F}F are "jump discontinuities". There are at most countably many such jumps. If furthermore F {F}F is bounded, one has a unique continuous-singular decomposition:

F=Fc+Fpp\displaystyle F=F_{c}+F_{pp}F=Fc​+Fpp​

where Fc {F_{c}}Fc​ is continuous non-decreasing and Fpp {F_{pp}}Fpp​ is a jump function. Combining this with a HL-type of inequality for Dini's numbers gives an important result of almost everywhere differentiablity for monotone functions:

Theorem 20 A monotone function F:R→R {F:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}}F:R→R is differentiable almost everywhere.

Much as we have Jordan decomposition for a signed measure, we have a decomposition result saying that any function of bounded variation can be written as a difference of two monotone functions. And thus the almost everywhere differentiablity extends to the function class of bounded variation. These "variations'' for both functions and measures are obviously related, via the Lebesgue-Radon-Nikodym theorem, which is manifested in the construction of Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure.
